== Mountain (the original form of a float) == [[File:Hikawa-jinjya_Akasaka10.JPG|thumb|200x200px|Parade of floats at the Akasaka Hikawa Festival [[Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)|Hikawa Shrine]] (Taken on 18 September 2010)]] [[File:Kagura_Tai_Float.jpg|thumb|285x285px|One of the three largest floats in Japan (a cart at the [[Takayama Festival]])]] [[File:Chichibu_Yomatsuri.jpg|thumb|200x200px|One of the three major hikiyama floats in Japan (Chichibu Night Festival floats)]][[File:Gion_Matsuri_2017-6a.jpg|thumb|301x301px|Long sword hoko of [[Gion Matsuri]], one of the three largest hoko in Japan, photographed on 17 July 2017.]] A {{Nihongo|mountain|山|yama}}is a substitute made to resemble a natural mountain and is used in festivals. The original form of a float.
In the ancient [[Folk religion|Folk belief]], there was a belief that gods descended from the heavens using rocks and trees on mountains and mountaintops as substitutes. These remain as [[Mountain worship]] or [[Shinto shrine]]s with mountains as [[Shintai]]. A typical example is [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Okami Shrine]] (Mt. Miwa). Even small shrines located at the foot of a mountain often have a [[Iwakura (Yorishiro)|Iwakura]] or [[Shinboku]] at the top.
As villages developed, rituals began to be held in the plains, and temporary shrines were established. At this time, a yorishiro was also set up to pray for the coming of the gods, and this became permanent, resulting in the establishment of facilities such as today's shrines. One of these substitutes is a mountain (yama, tsukuri yama or decorative yama) built to resemble a mountain. In addition to the permanent reliquaries inside the temples, these mountains came to be used at festivals as temporary reliquaries to express or reaffirm the descent of the gods. Originally, the mountain was actually built and prayed on, but later the altar came to be regarded as the mountain.
The first recorded mountain is "Mt. Aoba" in the article of [[Emperor Suinin|Taruhito]] in [[Kojiki]], where it is said that Kibisatsumi, the ancestor of the Izumo Kunizukuri, built a mountain decorated with green leaves as a garden to enshrine [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi]].
A rare example that retains the original meaning is the "Karasuyama no Yamaage event" (commonly known as "Yamaage Matsuri", a national [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]]) in [[Tochigi Prefecture]] [[Nasukarasuyama|Nasu Karasuyama City]].Originally, the festival involved the construction and dedication of an earthen mound in the town, but with the rise of the economy, the local specialty washi paper (Chomura-gami) was used to attach the mound to a frame made of wood and bamboo.The largest of these is 7 meters wide (the full width of the road) and over 10 meters high. At present, several floats and stage sets are combined over a depth of 100 meters, and entertainment (such as Kyogen and Kagura) is dedicated to the floats. These floats are paraded through the town just like other floats in other places. All of the floats are handmade, 7m wide, 10m high, and 100m deep, and the stage sets are assembled each time, entertained, dismantled, and moved up to 6 times a day, or 18 times in a 3-day festival. The waterfalls are painted on all of the mountains, in the hope that the blessings of the mountains will spread to all of the towns. Until the early Showa period (1926–1989), the mountains were burned at each festival and the ashes were given away as good luck charms.
The first mountain to be recorded as a form of ritual object is "Shirushi-no-Yama", which was pulled up for the [[Emperor Ninmyō|Nimei-tennō]]'s Great Lenten Festival in the 10th year of the [[Tenchō]] (833), November Boshin-jō in the [[Shoku Nihon Kōki|Chiku Nihon Kouki]]. (Shirushi-no-yama, Hyo-no-yama, Shime-yama), which was pulled during the Emperor Ninmyō It is said to be the original form of a float, with a role similar to that of a mobile shrine. There was a time when the festival was suspended, and the Shibeyama seems to have been abolished at that time.
The same type of floats appeared in folk festivals, and they were called "yokiyama," a type of float temporarily built like an altar, "hikiyama," a type of float pulled, and "kakiyama," a type of float carried. In the current festival, there are only a few floats that are not paraded, and most of them are paraded.
[The Hozutsu Hachimangu Shrine in [[Toyama Prefecture]] and the Futagami Imizu Shrine in [[Takaoka, Toyama|Takaoka City]] still perform the Tsukiyama event, a form of ancient worship. Although the origins of the Tsukiyama ritual are not well known, it is known that the Tsukiyama ritual at Hojozu Hachimangu Shrine has been performed since the early [[Edo period]], according to 1721 ([[Kyōhō|Kyōho]] in 1721 and "Tsukiyama Kooro Denki".
A temporary Tsukiyama ([[Altar]]) is set up in front of a large pine tree at Hōyūzu Hachimangu Shrine and three large cedar trees at Futagami Sagami Shrine to welcome the gods. Both mounts have a two-tiered altar, and the lower tier has two masks, one for each of the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] ([[Dhṛtarāṣṭra]], [[Virūḍhaka (Heavenly King)]], [[Virūpākṣa]], and [[Vaiśravaṇa]]), with a [[Karahafu]]-roofed temple ([[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper row. [[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper tier is a [[Karahafu]] roofed temple ([[Shrine]]). After the rituals are over, the mounds are dismantled in a great hurry according to the legend that each God is said to go berserk.
This event was also held at the Isurugihiko Shrine on [[Mount Sekidō|Ishidōzan]] in [[Noto (disambiguation)|Noto]], but was discontinued during the Meiji period. In Toyama Prefecture, the ceremony is performed only at Hōyūtsu Hachimangu Shrine and Futagami-Imizu Shrine, which was suspended in the Meiji period and revived in 1956 ([[Shōwa (1926-1989)|Showa]] 31). This is a rare event in Japan. Because of the appearance of the three main deities, it has been called "legless" in Houzu, "handless" in Futagamiyama, and "mouthless" in Ishidouyama.
== Danjiri == {{Nihongo|2=山車|3=Danjiri|4=lit "mountain vehicle"}} refers to traditional wooden festival floats, which can be classified as "hikiyama" (曳き山) that are pulled by people or "okiyama" (置き山) that are stationary. The most common type is the "hikiyama" with wheels, while the "okiyama" are placed at a fixed location. The names of the floats can be confusing since they vary and sometimes contradict each other across regions
The number of Danjiri has increased substantially in recent history in Japan. Danjiri have evolved as a form of entertainment and can be found in various forms throughout Japan. Although many have lost their original religious function, some still carry children or dolls, or incorporate objects used as substitutes in their decorations.
=== Structure === Depending on the region or district, there are many types of bogies with wheels inside or outside the bogie, wheels made of wood or metal, wheel size, and the way the wood of the bogie body is assembled.
; Wheel
The most common type of wheel is the four-wheeled one. There are two types of wheel: the yaguruma (spoked wheel) and itaguruma (board wheel) of the outer wheel style, and the inner wheel style. Some of them have lacquered or carved wheels, and some of them have auxiliary wheels. [The floats used in the [[Tenson Shrine|Otsu Festival]] in [[Shiga Prefecture]] and the [[Ishidori Matsuri]] in northern [[Mie Prefecture]] are three-wheeled, while those used in the [[Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka]], two-wheeled floats pulled in central and eastern [[Tōtōmi Province|Enshu]] from [[Mori, Shizuoka|Mori-cho]] to [[Iwata, Shizuoka|Iwata City]], six-wheeled floats such as Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, and [[Toyama Prefecture]] Some have six wheels, such as the Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, while others are sleigh-shaped without wheels, such as the Tatemon Festival in [[Uozu, Toyama|Uozu City]]. There are also different ways and forms of operation. In Ogi Gion, logs were laid one after another underneath the mountain without wheels, which was an unusual way of operating the festival, but now it is just a hikiyama with wheels.
; Power and means of transportation
In most cases, the floats are operated by human power. In rare cases, the floats are pulled by [[trucks]], or the floats themselves are powered, but this is a special case.
; Hikiyama (pulled mountain) Some of the floats have very elaborate [[Karakuri puppet]]s and vary in size from the size of an ordinary [[Mikoshi]] to more than ten times that size (weighing several tons). Among them, the hikiyama (big mountain) of the Aokashiwa Festival in Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, weighs about 20 tons and is said to be the largest in Japan. The reason for the creation of large floats is that they can be operated in a huge size due to the form of pulling, the remnants of the use of taller floats as a substitute, and competition between shrine parishioners as a style.
; Two-wheeled floats
A yatai is a float pulled by two wheels. Famous festivals include the Murakami Festival, the Enshu Yokosuka Mikumano Shrine Festival, and the Kakegawa Festival.
;Flower cart
This refers to all kinds of floats decorated with paper flowers and other floral decorations. In the Ofunato Festival, paper called "Ohana" is used to decorate the carts with gold and silver. All of these are used to fund the reconstruction of the shrine and the [[Kominkan|Community Center]].
;The ceremony was held at the [[Kaki-yama]] for carrying.
[[File:Saijou_matsuri_danjiri_siraki.JPG|thumb|A float for carrying at the Saijo Festival in Ehime Prefecture. It weighs about 800kg.]] This type of float is rare in Japan, and most of them weigh from a few hundred kilograms to about one or two tons at the heaviest. They are often confused with mikoshi (portable shrines), but they are classified as floats because of their nature as accompaniments to the Ujiko. One of the most famous is the [[Hakata Gion Yamakasa]].
=== Floats designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties === Of the festivals (events) still held throughout Japan, a total of 66 floats pulled at the following five festivals have been designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |title=国指定文化財等データベース |website=kunishitei.bunka.go.jp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120409223821/http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |archive-date=2012-04-09}} </ref>
All of the festivals in which they are pulled are listed on the [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] and on the [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]]. [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]] (see also the following section for more information on the festivals that have received this designation). At present, several floats and stage sets are combined over a depth of 100 meters, and entertainment (such as Kyogen and Kagura) is dedicated to the floats. These floats are paraded through the town just like other floats in other places. All of the floats are handmade, 7m wide, 10m high, and 100m deep, and the stage sets are assembled each time, entertained, dismantled, and moved up to 6 times a day, or 18 times in a 3-day festival. The waterfalls are painted on all of the mountains, in the hope that the blessings of the mountains will spread to all of the towns. The first mountain to be recorded as a form of ritual object is "Shirushi-no-Yama", which was pulled up for the [[Emperor Ninmyō|Nimei-tennō]]'s Great Lenten Festival in the 10th year of the [[Tenchō]] (833), November Boshin-jō in the [[Shoku Nihon Kōki|Chiku Nihon Kouki]]. (Shirushi-no-yama, Hyo-no-yama, Shime-yama), which was pulled during the Emperor Ninmyō It is said to be the original form of a float, with a role similar to that of a mobile shrine. There was a time when the festival was suspended, and the Shibeyama seems to have been abolished at that time.
The same type of floats appeared in folk festivals, and they were called "yokiyama," a type of float temporarily built like an altar, "hikiyama," a type of float pulled, and "kakiyama," a type of float carried. In the current festival, there are only a few floats that are not paraded, and most of them are paraded.
[The Hozutsu Hachimangu Shrine in [[Toyama Prefecture]] and the Futagami Imizu Shrine in [[Takaoka, Toyama|Takaoka City]] still perform the Tsukiyama event, a form of ancient worship. Although the origins of the Tsukiyama ritual are not well known, it is known that the Tsukiyama ritual at Hojozu Hachimangu Shrine has been performed since the early [[Edo period]], according to 1721 ([[Kyōhō|Kyōho]] in 1721 and "Tsukiyama Kooro Denki".
A temporary Tsukiyama ([[Altar]]) is set up in front of a large pine tree at Hōyūzu Hachimangu Shrine and three large cedar trees at Futagami Sagami Shrine to welcome the gods. Both mounts have a two-tiered altar, and the lower tier has two masks, one for each of the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] ([[Dhṛtarāṣṭra]], [[Virūḍhaka (Heavenly King)]], [[Virūpākṣa]], and [[Vaiśravaṇa]]), with a [[Karahafu]]-roofed temple ([[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper row. This is a rare event in Japan. Because of the appearance of the three main deities, it has been called "legless" in Houzu, "handless" in Futagamiyama, and "mouthless" in Ishidouyama.
== Danjiri == {{Nihongo|2=山車|3=Danjiri|4=lit "mountain vehicle"}} refers to traditional wooden festival floats, which can be classified as "hikiyama" (曳き山) that are pulled by people or "okiyama" (置き山) that are stationary. The most common type is the "hikiyama" with wheels, while the "okiyama" are placed at a fixed location. The names of the floats can be confusing since they vary and sometimes contradict each other across regions
The number of Danjiri has increased substantially in recent history in Japan. Danjiri have evolved as a form of entertainment and can be found in various forms throughout Japan. Although many have lost their original religious function, some still carry children or dolls, or incorporate objects used as substitutes in their decorations.
=== Structure === Depending on the region or district, there are many types of bogies with wheels inside or outside the bogie, wheels made of wood or metal, wheel size, and the way the wood of the bogie body is assembled.
; Wheel
The most common type of wheel is the four-wheeled one. There are two types of wheel: the yaguruma (spoked wheel) and itaguruma (board wheel) of the outer wheel style, and the inner wheel style. Some of them have lacquered or carved wheels, and some of them have auxiliary wheels. [The floats used in the [[Tenson Shrine|Otsu Festival]] in [[Shiga Prefecture]] and the [[Ishidori Matsuri]] in northern [[Mie Prefecture]] are three-wheeled, while those used in the [[Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka]], two-wheeled floats pulled in central and eastern [[Tōtōmi Province|Enshu]] from [[Mori, Shizuoka|Mori-cho]] to [[Iwata, Shizuoka|Iwata City]], six-wheeled floats such as Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, and [[Toyama Prefecture]] Some have six wheels, such as the Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, while others are sleigh-shaped without wheels, such as the Tatemon Festival in [[Uozu, Toyama|Uozu City]]. There are also different ways and forms of operation. In Ogi Gion, logs were laid one after another underneath the mountain without wheels, which was an unusual way of operating the festival, but now it is just a hikiyama with wheels.
; Power and means of transportation
In most cases, the floats are operated by human power. In rare cases, the floats are pulled by [[trucks]], or the floats themselves are powered, but this is a special case.
; Hikiyama (pulled mountain) Some of the floats have very elaborate [[Karakuri puppet]]s and vary in size from the size of an ordinary [[Mikoshi]] to more than ten times that size (weighing several tons). Among them, the hikiyama (big mountain) of the Aokashiwa Festival in Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, weighs about 20 tons and is said to be the largest in Japan. The reason for the creation of large floats is that they can be operated in a huge size due to the form of pulling, the remnants of the use of taller floats as a substitute, and competition between shrine parishioners as a style.
; Two-wheeled floats
A yatai is a float pulled by two wheels. Famous festivals include the Murakami Festival, the Enshu Yokosuka Mikumano Shrine Festival, and the Kakegawa Festival.
;Flower cart
This refers to all kinds of floats decorated with paper flowers and other floral decorations. In the Ofunato Festival, paper called "Ohana" is used to decorate the carts with gold and silver. All of these are used to fund the reconstruction of the shrine and the [[Kominkan|Community Center]].
;The ceremony was held at the [[Kaki-yama]] for carrying.
[[File:Saijou_matsuri_danjiri_siraki.JPG|thumb|A float for carrying at the Saijo Festival in Ehime Prefecture. It weighs about 800kg.]] This type of float is rare in Japan, and most of them weigh from a few hundred kilograms to about one or two tons at the heaviest. They are often confused with mikoshi (portable shrines), but they are classified as floats because of their nature as accompaniments to the Ujiko. One of the most famous is the [[Hakata Gion Yamakasa]].
=== Floats designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties === Of the festivals (events) still held throughout Japan, a total of 66 floats pulled at the following five festivals have been designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |title=国指定文化財等データベース |website=kunishitei.bunka.go.jp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120409223821/http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |archive-date=2012-04-09}} </ref>
All of the festivals in which they are pulled are listed on the [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] and on the [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]]. [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]] (see also the following section for more information on the festivals that have received this designation). {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}} {{Overly detailed|date=April 2022}}[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] A {{nihongo|'''matsuri float'''|山車|dashi {{noitalic|''or''}} sansha}} is a general term for a [[Float (parade)|float]] that is pulled or carried during a [[Matsuri|festival]] in Japan.
Dashi are one of three large structures at [[Japanese festivals]] alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=MATCHA |title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia |url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE |language=en}}</ref>
Terminology is inconsistent and varies by region. Some of the most common names include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. In addition, dashi and yatai are sometimes referred to as hikiyama and yama.<ref name=":0" /> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people.]] Dashi floats (山車) are an essential part of Japanese festivals and originally made to resemble mountains. It reflects minkan shinko or folk religion, where people believed that spirits lived in the mountains. The spears and swords adorning the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride atop the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people and allowed to carry passengers.<ref name=":0" />
By contrast Mikoshi serve a function of carrying kami in a procession called a {{Interlanguage link|Shinkō-sai|ja|神幸祭|simple|Shinko-shiki}}. A Mikoshi is carried on people's shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is reserved for gods.<ref name=":0" />
There are several festivals where one can see dashi floats, including the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi weave through the city, both during the day and in the evening. The Kanda Matsuri features dashi floats and mikoshi, with people dressed up in traditional costumes parading through the streets.<ref name=":0" />
== Another name for floats == It is called in various ways depending on the region.
=== Yama no tsukemono ===
* '''Yamahama''' (mountain, float, obstacle), '''Hikiyama''' (pulling mountain, towing mountain), '''Kakiyama''' (carrying mountain, carrying mountain). * '''Yamaboko''' (Yamaboko). A float with a structure in the shape of a mountain on a stand, and a [[Hoko yari]] or long sword.<ref>『大辞泉』</ref>。From the legend that evil gods are attracted to shiny things like spears.<ref>[http://www7b.biglobe.ne.jp/~bukatucenter/0809aki.pdf 戦国時代の祇園祭] カトリック大阪教会管区部落問題活動センター事務局、2008年9月</ref>。 * '''Yamakasa''' (Yamakasa) (Northern [[Kyusyu|Kyushu]] region) * '''Yatai''' (floats) (Shinjo City, Yamagata Prefecture, Mogami region)
=== Things with cars (except the above) ===
* '''Danjiri''' (Jidaijiri, Daijiri, Danjiri, Kururaku, Danjiri)<ref>牧村史陽・編『大阪ことば事典』講談社（講談社文庫）1998年、415,416頁。</ref>）([[Kansai region|Kinki region]], [[Chūgoku region|China region]], [[Shikoku region]]) * '''Saisha''' (festival car) ([[Mie Prefecture]], [[Kuwana, Mie|Kuwana City]] region) * '''Okuruma''' (carts) from the [[Chita Peninsula|Chita Region]] and [[Owari Province|Owari]] regions.
=== Kasabo (kasa) (excluding the above) ===
* '''Kasaboko''' ('''Kasaboko''') (Chichibu region, etc.) * '''Okasa'''' ([[Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe City]])
=== Objects of the platform ===
* '''Yatai''' (food stalls) (mainly in [[Chūbu region|Chubu region]] such as [[Nagano Prefecture]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], Enshu, [[Gifu Prefecture]], [[Hida, Gifu|Hida]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]), [[Odawara]] City and [[Hyogo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]], the Harima region, [[Iwate Prefecture]], inland and coastal inland regions.) * '''Taiko-dai''' (drum stands) (mainly in the [[Setouchi region|Setouchi Prefecture]], including [[Niihama]] City, [[Saijō, Ehime|Saijo City]], [[Yao, Osaka|Yao City, Osaka Prefecture]], and [[Sakai]] City in Ehime Prefecture) * {{nihongo|'''Daigaku'''|台楽, 台額}} (There were Daigaku throughout the southern part of Osaka City before the war, but as of 2015, there are only two at Ikune Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-12-15 |title=女子も奮闘 大阪・生根神社 夜空を焦がす巨大「だいがく」 {{!}} THE PAGE 大阪 |url=http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |access-date=2022-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151215054331/http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |archive-date=15 December 2015 }}</ref>)
The word '''dashi''' is derived from two theories: one is that it is a display outside the temple or precincts, and the other is that it is a display of [[Yorishiro]], the beard basket. The word "yama" refers to all kinds of floats, but the word "kuruma" is often used to refer to hikiyama.

Among them, the hikiyama (big mountain) of the Aokashiwa Festival in Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, weighs about 20 tons and is said to be the largest in Japan. The reason for the creation of large floats is that they can be operated in a huge size due to the form of pulling, the remnants of the use of taller floats as a substitute, and competition between shrine parishioners as a style.
; Two-wheeled floats
A yatai is a float pulled by two wheels. Famous festivals include the Murakami Festival, the Enshu Yokosuka Mikumano Shrine Festival, and the Kakegawa Festival.
;Flower cart
This refers to all kinds of floats decorated with paper flowers and other floral decorations. In the Ofunato Festival, paper called "Ohana" is used to decorate the carts with gold and silver. All of these are used to fund the reconstruction of the shrine and the [[Kominkan|Community Center]].
;The ceremony was held at the [[Kaki-yama]] for carrying.
[[File:Saijou_matsuri_danjiri_siraki.JPG|thumb|A float for carrying at the Saijo Festival in Ehime Prefecture. It weighs about 800kg.]] This type of float is rare in Japan, and most of them weigh from a few hundred kilograms to about one or two tons at the heaviest. They are often confused with mikoshi (portable shrines), but they are classified as floats because of their nature as accompaniments to the Ujiko. One of the most famous is the [[Hakata Gion Yamakasa]].

All of the festivals in which they are pulled are listed on the [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] and on the [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]]. {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}} {{Overly detailed|date=April 2022}}[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding to welcome the gods. Note the wheels and people pulling it]] A {{nihongo|'''matsuri float'''|山車|dashi {{noitalic|''or''}} sansha}} is a general term for a [[Float (parade)|float]] that is pulled or carried during a [[Matsuri|festival]] in Japan.
Dashi are one of three large structures at [[Japanese festivals]] alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=MATCHA |title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia |url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE |language=en}}</ref>
Terminology is inconsistent and varies by region. Some of the most common names include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. In addition, dashi and yatai are sometimes referred to as hikiyama and yama.<ref name=":0" /> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people. Note the lack of wheels or human occupants]] Dashi floats (山車) are an essential part of Japanese festivals and originally made to resemble mountains. It reflects minkan shinko or folk religion, where people believed that spirits lived in the mountains. The spears and swords adorning the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride atop the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people and allowed to carry passengers.<ref name=":0" />
By contrast Mikoshi serve a function of carrying kami in a procession called a {{Interlanguage link|Shinkō-sai|ja|神幸祭|simple|Shinko-shiki}}. A Mikoshi is carried on people's shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is reserved for gods.<ref name=":0" />
There are several festivals where one can see dashi floats, including the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi weave through the city, both during the day and in the evening. The Kanda Matsuri features dashi floats and mikoshi, with people dressed up in traditional costumes parading through the streets.<ref name=":0" />
== Another name for floats == It is called in various ways depending on the region.
=== Yama no tsukemono ===
* '''Yamahama''' (mountain, float, obstacle), '''Hikiyama''' (pulling mountain, towing mountain), '''Kakiyama''' (carrying mountain, carrying mountain). * '''Yamaboko''' (Yamaboko). A float with a structure in the shape of a mountain on a stand, and a [[Hoko yari]] or long sword.<ref>『大辞泉』</ref>。From the legend that evil gods are attracted to shiny things like spears.<ref>[http://www7b.biglobe.ne.jp/~bukatucenter/0809aki.pdf 戦国時代の祇園祭] カトリック大阪教会管区部落問題活動センター事務局、2008年9月</ref>。 * '''Yamakasa''' (Yamakasa) (Northern [[Kyusyu|Kyushu]] region) * '''Yatai''' (floats) (Shinjo City, Yamagata Prefecture, Mogami region)
=== Things with cars (except the above) ===
* '''Danjiri''' (Jidaijiri, Daijiri, Danjiri, Kururaku, Danjiri)<ref>牧村史陽・編『大阪ことば事典』講談社（講談社文庫）1998年、415,416頁。</ref>）([[Kansai region|Kinki region]], [[Chūgoku region|China region]], [[Shikoku region]]) * '''Saisha''' (festival car) ([[Mie Prefecture]], [[Kuwana, Mie|Kuwana City]] region) * '''Okuruma''' (carts) from the [[Chita Peninsula|Chita Region]] and [[Owari Province|Owari]] regions.
=== Kasabo (kasa) (excluding the above) ===

=== Objects of the platform ===
* '''Yatai''' (food stalls) (mainly in [[Chūbu region|Chubu region]] such as [[Nagano Prefecture]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], Enshu, [[Gifu Prefecture]], [[Hida, Gifu|Hida]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]), [[Odawara]] City and [[Hyogo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]], the Harima region, [[Iwate Prefecture]], inland and coastal inland regions.) * '''Taiko-dai''' (drum stands) (mainly in the [[Setouchi region|Setouchi Prefecture]], including [[Niihama]] City, [[Saijō, Ehime|Saijo City]], [[Yao, Osaka|Yao City, Osaka Prefecture]], and [[Sakai]] City in Ehime Prefecture) * {{nihongo|'''Daigaku'''|台楽, 台額}} (There were Daigaku throughout the southern part of Osaka City before the war, but as of 2015, there are only two at Ikune Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-12-15 |title=女子も奮闘 大阪・生根神社 夜空を焦がす巨大「だいがく」 {{!}} THE PAGE 大阪 |url=http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |access-date=2022-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151215054331/http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |archive-date=15 December 2015 }}</ref>)
The word '''dashi''' is derived from two theories: one is that it is a display outside the temple or precincts, and the other is that it is a display of [[Yorishiro]], the beard basket. The word "yama" refers to all kinds of floats, but the word "kuruma" is often used to refer to hikiyama.
== Mountain (the original form of a float) == [[File:Hikawa-jinjya_Akasaka10.JPG|thumb|200x200px|Parade of floats at the Akasaka Hikawa Festival [[Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)|Hikawa Shrine]] (Taken on 18 September 2010)]] [[File:Kagura_Tai_Float.jpg|thumb|285x285px|One of the three largest floats in Japan (a cart at the [[Takayama Festival]])]] [[File:Chichibu_Yomatsuri.jpg|thumb|200x200px|One of the three major hikiyama floats in Japan (Chichibu Night Festival floats)]][[File:Gion_Matsuri_2017-6a.jpg|thumb|301x301px|Long sword hoko of [[Gion Matsuri]], one of the three largest hoko in Japan, photographed on 17 July 2017.]] A {{Nihongo|mountain|山|yama}}is a substitute made to resemble a natural mountain and is used in festivals. The original form of a float.
In the ancient [[Folk religion|Folk belief]], there was a belief that gods descended from the heavens using rocks and trees on mountains and mountaintops as substitutes. These remain as [[Mountain worship]] or [[Shinto shrine]]s with mountains as [[Shintai]]. A typical example is [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Okami Shrine]] (Mt. Miwa). Even small shrines located at the foot of a mountain often have a [[Iwakura (Yorishiro)|Iwakura]] or [[Shinboku]] at the top.
As villages developed, rituals began to be held in the plains, and temporary shrines were established. At this time, a yorishiro was also set up to pray for the coming of the gods, and this became permanent, resulting in the establishment of facilities such as today's shrines. One of these substitutes is a mountain (yama, tsukuri yama or decorative yama) built to resemble a mountain. In addition to the permanent reliquaries inside the temples, these mountains came to be used at festivals as temporary reliquaries to express or reaffirm the descent of the gods. Originally, the mountain was actually built and prayed on, but later the altar came to be regarded as the mountain.
The first recorded mountain is "Mt. Aoba" in the article of [[Emperor Suinin|Taruhito]] in [[Kojiki]], where it is said that Kibisatsumi, the ancestor of the Izumo Kunizukuri, built a mountain decorated with green leaves as a garden to enshrine [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi]].
A rare example that retains the original meaning is the "Karasuyama no Yamaage event" (commonly known as "Yamaage Matsuri", a national [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]]) in [[Tochigi Prefecture]] [[Nasukarasuyama|Nasu Karasuyama City]].Originally, the festival involved the construction and dedication of an earthen mound in the town, but with the rise of the economy, the local specialty washi paper (Chomura-gami) was used to attach the mound to a frame made of wood and bamboo.The largest of these is 7 meters wide (the full width of the road) and over 10 meters high. At present, several floats and stage sets are combined over a depth of 100 meters, and entertainment (such as Kyogen and Kagura) is dedicated to the floats. These floats are paraded through the town just like other floats in other places. All of the floats are handmade, 7m wide, 10m high, and 100m deep, and the stage sets are assembled each time, entertained, dismantled, and moved up to 6 times a day, or 18 times in a 3-day festival. The waterfalls are painted on all of the mountains, in the hope that the blessings of the mountains will spread to all of the towns. Until the early Showa period (1926–1989), the mountains were burned at each festival and the ashes were given away as good luck charms.
The first mountain to be recorded as a form of ritual object is "Shirushi-no-Yama", which was pulled up for the [[Emperor Ninmyō|Nimei-tennō]]'s Great Lenten Festival in the 10th year of the [[Tenchō]] (833), November Boshin-jō in the [[Shoku Nihon Kōki|Chiku Nihon Kouki]]. (Shirushi-no-yama, Hyo-no-yama, Shime-yama), which was pulled during the Emperor Ninmyō It is said to be the original form of a float, with a role similar to that of a mobile shrine. There was a time when the festival was suspended, and the Shibeyama seems to have been abolished at that time.
The same type of floats appeared in folk festivals, and they were called "yokiyama," a type of float temporarily built like an altar, "hikiyama," a type of float pulled, and "kakiyama," a type of float carried. In the current festival, there are only a few floats that are not paraded, and most of them are paraded.
[The Hozutsu Hachimangu Shrine in [[Toyama Prefecture]] and the Futagami Imizu Shrine in [[Takaoka, Toyama|Takaoka City]] still perform the Tsukiyama event, a form of ancient worship. Although the origins of the Tsukiyama ritual are not well known, it is known that the Tsukiyama ritual at Hojozu Hachimangu Shrine has been performed since the early [[Edo period]], according to 1721 ([[Kyōhō|Kyōho]] in 1721 and "Tsukiyama Kooro Denki".
A temporary Tsukiyama ([[Altar]]) is set up in front of a large pine tree at Hōyūzu Hachimangu Shrine and three large cedar trees at Futagami Sagami Shrine to welcome the gods. Both mounts have a two-tiered altar, and the lower tier has two masks, one for each of the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] ([[Dhṛtarāṣṭra]], [[Virūḍhaka (Heavenly King)]], [[Virūpākṣa]], and [[Vaiśravaṇa]]), with a [[Karahafu]]-roofed temple ([[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper row. [[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper tier is a [[Karahafu]] roofed temple ([[Shrine]]). After the rituals are over, the mounds are dismantled in a great hurry according to the legend that each God is said to go berserk.
This event was also held at the Isurugihiko Shrine on [[Mount Sekidō|Ishidōzan]] in [[Noto (disambiguation)|Noto]], but was discontinued during the Meiji period. In Toyama Prefecture, the ceremony is performed only at Hōyūtsu Hachimangu Shrine and Futagami-Imizu Shrine, which was suspended in the Meiji period and revived in 1956 ([[Shōwa (1926-1989)|Showa]] 31). This is a rare event in Japan. Because of the appearance of the three main deities, it has been called "legless" in Houzu, "handless" in Futagamiyama, and "mouthless" in Ishidouyama.
== Danjiri == {{Nihongo|2=山車|3=Danjiri|4=lit "mountain vehicle"}} refers to traditional wooden festival floats, which can be classified as "hikiyama" (曳き山) that are pulled by people or "okiyama" (置き山) that are stationary. The most common type is the "hikiyama" with wheels, while the "okiyama" are placed at a fixed location. The names of the floats can be confusing since they vary and sometimes contradict each other across regions
The number of Danjiri has increased substantially in recent history in Japan. Danjiri have evolved as a form of entertainment and can be found in various forms throughout Japan. Although many have lost their original religious function, some still carry children or dolls, or incorporate objects used as substitutes in their decorations.
=== Structure === Depending on the region or district, there are many types of bogies with wheels inside or outside the bogie, wheels made of wood or metal, wheel size, and the way the wood of the bogie body is assembled.
; Wheel
The most common type of wheel is the four-wheeled one. There are two types of wheel: the yaguruma (spoked wheel) and itaguruma (board wheel) of the outer wheel style, and the inner wheel style. Some of them have lacquered or carved wheels, and some of them have auxiliary wheels. [The floats used in the [[Tenson Shrine|Otsu Festival]] in [[Shiga Prefecture]] and the [[Ishidori Matsuri]] in northern [[Mie Prefecture]] are three-wheeled, while those used in the [[Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka]], two-wheeled floats pulled in central and eastern [[Tōtōmi Province|Enshu]] from [[Mori, Shizuoka|Mori-cho]] to [[Iwata, Shizuoka|Iwata City]], six-wheeled floats such as Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, and [[Toyama Prefecture]] Some have six wheels, such as the Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, while others are sleigh-shaped without wheels, such as the Tatemon Festival in [[Uozu, Toyama|Uozu City]]. There are also different ways and forms of operation. In Ogi Gion, logs were laid one after another underneath the mountain without wheels, which was an unusual way of operating the festival, but now it is just a hikiyama with wheels.
; Power and means of transportation
In most cases, the floats are operated by human power. In rare cases, the floats are pulled by [[trucks]], or the floats themselves are powered, but this is a special case.
; Hikiyama (pulled mountain) Some of the floats have very elaborate [[Karakuri puppet]]s and vary in size from the size of an ordinary [[Mikoshi]] to more than ten times that size (weighing several tons). Among them, the hikiyama (big mountain) of the Aokashiwa Festival in Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, weighs about 20 tons and is said to be the largest in Japan. The reason for the creation of large floats is that they can be operated in a huge size due to the form of pulling, the remnants of the use of taller floats as a substitute, and competition between shrine parishioners as a style.
; Two-wheeled floats
A yatai is a float pulled by two wheels. Famous festivals include the Murakami Festival, the Enshu Yokosuka Mikumano Shrine Festival, and the Kakegawa Festival.
;Flower cart
This refers to all kinds of floats decorated with paper flowers and other floral decorations. In the Ofunato Festival, paper called "Ohana" is used to decorate the carts with gold and silver. All of these are used to fund the reconstruction of the shrine and the [[Kominkan|Community Center]].

It weighs about 800kg.]] This type of float is rare in Japan, and most of them weigh from a few hundred kilograms to about one or two tons at the heaviest. {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}} {{Overly detailed|date=April 2022}}[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding to welcome the gods. Note the wheels and people pulling it]] A {{nihongo|'''matsuri float'''|山車|dashi {{noitalic|''or''}} sansha}} is a general term for a [[Float (parade)|float]] that is pulled or carried during a [[Matsuri|festival]] in Japan.
Dashi are one of three large structures at [[Japanese festivals]] alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=MATCHA |title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia |url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE |language=en}}</ref>
Terminology is inconsistent and varies by region. Some of the most common names include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. In addition, dashi and yatai are sometimes referred to as hikiyama and yama.<ref name=":0" /> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people. Note the lack of wheels or human occupants]] Dashi floats (山車) are an essential part of Japanese festivals and originally made to resemble mountains. It reflects minkan shinko or folk religion, where people believed that spirits lived in the mountains. The spears and swords adorning the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride atop the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people and allowed to carry passengers.<ref name=":0" />
By contrast Mikoshi serve a function of carrying kami in a procession called a {{Interlanguage link|Shinkō-sai|ja|神幸祭|simple|Shinko-shiki}}. A Mikoshi is carried on people's shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is reserved for gods.<ref name=":0" />
There are several festivals where one can see dashi floats, including the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi weave through the city, both during the day and in the evening. The Kanda Matsuri features dashi floats and mikoshi, with people dressed up in traditional costumes parading through the streets.<ref name=":0" />
== Another name for floats == It is called in various ways depending on the region.
=== Yama no tsukemono ===
* '''Yamahama''' (mountain, float, obstacle), '''Hikiyama''' (pulling mountain, towing mountain), '''Kakiyama''' (carrying mountain, carrying mountain). * '''Yamaboko''' (Yamaboko). A float with a structure in the shape of a mountain on a stand, and a [[Hoko yari]] or long sword.<ref>『大辞泉』</ref>。From the legend that evil gods are attracted to shiny things like spears.<ref>[http://www7b.biglobe.ne.jp/~bukatucenter/0809aki.pdf 戦国時代の祇園祭] カトリック大阪教会管区部落問題活動センター事務局、2008年9月</ref>。 * '''Yamakasa''' (Yamakasa) (Northern [[Kyusyu|Kyushu]] region) * '''Yatai''' (floats) (Shinjo City, Yamagata Prefecture, Mogami region)
=== Things with cars (except the above) ===
* '''Danjiri''' (Jidaijiri, Daijiri, Danjiri, Kururaku, Danjiri)<ref>牧村史陽・編『大阪ことば事典』講談社（講談社文庫）1998年、415,416頁。</ref>）([[Kansai region|Kinki region]], [[Chūgoku region|China region]], [[Shikoku region]]) * '''Saisha''' (festival car) ([[Mie Prefecture]], [[Kuwana, Mie|Kuwana City]] region) * '''Okuruma''' (carts) from the [[Chita Peninsula|Chita Region]] and [[Owari Province|Owari]] regions.
=== Kasabo (kasa) (excluding the above) ===
* '''Kasaboko''' ('''Kasaboko''') (Chichibu region, etc.) * '''Okasa'''' ([[Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Tanabe, Wakayama|Tanabe City]])
=== Objects of the platform ===
* '''Yatai''' (food stalls) (mainly in [[Chūbu region|Chubu region]] such as [[Nagano Prefecture]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]], Enshu, [[Gifu Prefecture]], [[Hida, Gifu|Hida]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]]), [[Odawara]] City and [[Hyogo Prefecture|Hyōgo Prefecture]], the Harima region, [[Iwate Prefecture]], inland and coastal inland regions.) * '''Taiko-dai''' (drum stands) (mainly in the [[Setouchi region|Setouchi Prefecture]], including [[Niihama]] City, [[Saijō, Ehime|Saijo City]], [[Yao, Osaka|Yao City, Osaka Prefecture]], and [[Sakai]] City in Ehime Prefecture) * {{nihongo|'''Daigaku'''|台楽, 台額}} (There were Daigaku throughout the southern part of Osaka City before the war, but as of 2015, there are only two at Ikune Shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-12-15 |title=女子も奮闘 大阪・生根神社 夜空を焦がす巨大「だいがく」 {{!}} THE PAGE 大阪 |url=http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |access-date=2022-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151215054331/http://osaka.thepage.jp/detail/20150729-00000001-wordleafv |archive-date=15 December 2015 }}</ref>)
The word '''dashi''' is derived from two theories: one is that it is a display outside the temple or precincts, and the other is that it is a display of [[Yorishiro]], the beard basket. The word "yama" refers to all kinds of floats, but the word "kuruma" is often used to refer to hikiyama.
== Mountain (the original form of a float) == [[File:Hikawa-jinjya_Akasaka10.JPG|thumb|200x200px|Parade of floats at the Akasaka Hikawa Festival [[Hikawa Shrine (Akasaka)|Hikawa Shrine]] (Taken on 18 September 2010)]] [[File:Kagura_Tai_Float.jpg|thumb|285x285px|One of the three largest floats in Japan (a cart at the [[Takayama Festival]])]] [[File:Chichibu_Yomatsuri.jpg|thumb|200x200px|One of the three major hikiyama floats in Japan (Chichibu Night Festival floats)]][[File:Gion_Matsuri_2017-6a.jpg|thumb|301x301px|Long sword hoko of [[Gion Matsuri]], one of the three largest hoko in Japan, photographed on 17 July 2017.]] A {{Nihongo|mountain|山|yama}}is a substitute made to resemble a natural mountain and is used in festivals. The original form of a float.
In the ancient [[Folk religion|Folk belief]], there was a belief that gods descended from the heavens using rocks and trees on mountains and mountaintops as substitutes. These remain as [[Mountain worship]] or [[Shinto shrine]]s with mountains as [[Shintai]]. A typical example is [[Ōmiwa Shrine|Okami Shrine]] (Mt. Miwa). Even small shrines located at the foot of a mountain often have a [[Iwakura (Yorishiro)|Iwakura]] or [[Shinboku]] at the top.
As villages developed, rituals began to be held in the plains, and temporary shrines were established. At this time, a yorishiro was also set up to pray for the coming of the gods, and this became permanent, resulting in the establishment of facilities such as today's shrines. One of these substitutes is a mountain (yama, tsukuri yama or decorative yama) built to resemble a mountain. In addition to the permanent reliquaries inside the temples, these mountains came to be used at festivals as temporary reliquaries to express or reaffirm the descent of the gods. Originally, the mountain was actually built and prayed on, but later the altar came to be regarded as the mountain.
The first recorded mountain is "Mt. Aoba" in the article of [[Emperor Suinin|Taruhito]] in [[Kojiki]], where it is said that Kibisatsumi, the ancestor of the Izumo Kunizukuri, built a mountain decorated with green leaves as a garden to enshrine [[Ōkuninushi|Okuninushi]].
A rare example that retains the original meaning is the "Karasuyama no Yamaage event" (commonly known as "Yamaage Matsuri", a national [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]]) in [[Tochigi Prefecture]] [[Nasukarasuyama|Nasu Karasuyama City]].Originally, the festival involved the construction and dedication of an earthen mound in the town, but with the rise of the economy, the local specialty washi paper (Chomura-gami) was used to attach the mound to a frame made of wood and bamboo.The largest of these is 7 meters wide (the full width of the road) and over 10 meters high. At present, several floats and stage sets are combined over a depth of 100 meters, and entertainment (such as Kyogen and Kagura) is dedicated to the floats. These floats are paraded through the town just like other floats in other places. All of the floats are handmade, 7m wide, 10m high, and 100m deep, and the stage sets are assembled each time, entertained, dismantled, and moved up to 6 times a day, or 18 times in a 3-day festival. The waterfalls are painted on all of the mountains, in the hope that the blessings of the mountains will spread to all of the towns. Until the early Showa period (1926–1989), the mountains were burned at each festival and the ashes were given away as good luck charms.
The first mountain to be recorded as a form of ritual object is "Shirushi-no-Yama", which was pulled up for the [[Emperor Ninmyō|Nimei-tennō]]'s Great Lenten Festival in the 10th year of the [[Tenchō]] (833), November Boshin-jō in the [[Shoku Nihon Kōki|Chiku Nihon Kouki]]. (Shirushi-no-yama, Hyo-no-yama, Shime-yama), which was pulled during the Emperor Ninmyō It is said to be the original form of a float, with a role similar to that of a mobile shrine. There was a time when the festival was suspended, and the Shibeyama seems to have been abolished at that time.
The same type of floats appeared in folk festivals, and they were called "yokiyama," a type of float temporarily built like an altar, "hikiyama," a type of float pulled, and "kakiyama," a type of float carried. In the current festival, there are only a few floats that are not paraded, and most of them are paraded.
[The Hozutsu Hachimangu Shrine in [[Toyama Prefecture]] and the Futagami Imizu Shrine in [[Takaoka, Toyama|Takaoka City]] still perform the Tsukiyama event, a form of ancient worship. Although the origins of the Tsukiyama ritual are not well known, it is known that the Tsukiyama ritual at Hojozu Hachimangu Shrine has been performed since the early [[Edo period]], according to 1721 ([[Kyōhō|Kyōho]] in 1721 and "Tsukiyama Kooro Denki".
A temporary Tsukiyama ([[Altar]]) is set up in front of a large pine tree at Hōyūzu Hachimangu Shrine and three large cedar trees at Futagami Sagami Shrine to welcome the gods. Both mounts have a two-tiered altar, and the lower tier has two masks, one for each of the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] ([[Dhṛtarāṣṭra]], [[Virūḍhaka (Heavenly King)]], [[Virūpākṣa]], and [[Vaiśravaṇa]]), with a [[Karahafu]]-roofed temple ([[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper row. [[Hokora]]) in the center of the upper tier is a [[Karahafu]] roofed temple ([[Shrine]]). After the rituals are over, the mounds are dismantled in a great hurry according to the legend that each God is said to go berserk.
This event was also held at the Isurugihiko Shrine on [[Mount Sekidō|Ishidōzan]] in [[Noto (disambiguation)|Noto]], but was discontinued during the Meiji period. In Toyama Prefecture, the ceremony is performed only at Hōyūtsu Hachimangu Shrine and Futagami-Imizu Shrine, which was suspended in the Meiji period and revived in 1956 ([[Shōwa (1926-1989)|Showa]] 31). This is a rare event in Japan. Because of the appearance of the three main deities, it has been called "legless" in Houzu, "handless" in Futagamiyama, and "mouthless" in Ishidouyama.
== Danjiri == {{Nihongo|2=山車|3=Danjiri|4=lit "mountain vehicle"}} refers to traditional wooden festival floats, which can be classified as "hikiyama" (曳き山) that are pulled by people or "okiyama" (置き山) that are stationary. The most common type is the "hikiyama" with wheels, while the "okiyama" are placed at a fixed location. The names of the floats can be confusing since they vary and sometimes contradict each other across regions
The number of Danjiri has increased substantially in recent history in Japan. Danjiri have evolved as a form of entertainment and can be found in various forms throughout Japan. Although many have lost their original religious function, some still carry children or dolls, or incorporate objects used as substitutes in their decorations.
=== Structure === Depending on the region or district, there are many types of bogies with wheels inside or outside the bogie, wheels made of wood or metal, wheel size, and the way the wood of the bogie body is assembled.
; Wheel
The most common type of wheel is the four-wheeled one. There are two types of wheel: the yaguruma (spoked wheel) and itaguruma (board wheel) of the outer wheel style, and the inner wheel style. Some of them have lacquered or carved wheels, and some of them have auxiliary wheels. [The floats used in the [[Tenson Shrine|Otsu Festival]] in [[Shiga Prefecture]] and the [[Ishidori Matsuri]] in northern [[Mie Prefecture]] are three-wheeled, while those used in the [[Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka]], two-wheeled floats pulled in central and eastern [[Tōtōmi Province|Enshu]] from [[Mori, Shizuoka|Mori-cho]] to [[Iwata, Shizuoka|Iwata City]], six-wheeled floats such as Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, and [[Toyama Prefecture]] Some have six wheels, such as the Hamasaki Gion Yamakasa, while others are sleigh-shaped without wheels, such as the Tatemon Festival in [[Uozu, Toyama|Uozu City]]. There are also different ways and forms of operation. In Ogi Gion, logs were laid one after another underneath the mountain without wheels, which was an unusual way of operating the festival, but now it is just a hikiyama with wheels.
; Power and means of transportation
In most cases, the floats are operated by human power. In rare cases, the floats are pulled by [[trucks]], or the floats themselves are powered, but this is a special case.
; Hikiyama (pulled mountain) Some of the floats have very elaborate [[Karakuri puppet]]s and vary in size from the size of an ordinary [[Mikoshi]] to more than ten times that size (weighing several tons). Among them, the hikiyama (big mountain) of the Aokashiwa Festival in Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, weighs about 20 tons and is said to be the largest in Japan. The reason for the creation of large floats is that they can be operated in a huge size due to the form of pulling, the remnants of the use of taller floats as a substitute, and competition between shrine parishioners as a style.
; Two-wheeled floats
A yatai is a float pulled by two wheels. Famous festivals include the Murakami Festival, the Enshu Yokosuka Mikumano Shrine Festival, and the Kakegawa Festival.
;Flower cart
This refers to all kinds of floats decorated with paper flowers and other floral decorations. In the Ofunato Festival, paper called "Ohana" is used to decorate the carts with gold and silver. All of these are used to fund the reconstruction of the shrine and the [[Kominkan|Community Center]].
;The ceremony was held at the [[Kaki-yama]] for carrying.
[[File:Saijou_matsuri_danjiri_siraki.JPG|thumb|A float for carrying at the Saijo Festival in Ehime Prefecture. It weighs about 800kg.]] This type of float is rare in Japan, and most of them weigh from a few hundred kilograms to about one or two tons at the heaviest. They are often confused with mikoshi (portable shrines), but they are classified as floats because of their nature as accompaniments to the Ujiko. One of the most famous is the [[Hakata Gion Yamakasa]].
=== Floats designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties === Of the festivals (events) still held throughout Japan, a total of 66 floats pulled at the following five festivals have been designated as Important Tangible Folk Cultural Properties.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |title=国指定文化財等データベース |website=kunishitei.bunka.go.jp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120409223821/http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index_pc.asp |archive-date=2012-04-09}} </ref>
All of the festivals in which they are pulled are listed on the [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] and on the [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]]. [[Intangible cultural heritage]] of [[UNESCO]] (see also the following section for more information on the festivals that have received this designation). {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}} [[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] A Matsuri float, also known as a dashi or sansha, is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose. Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside Yatai, and [[Mikoshi]].{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}} The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}MATCHA. [https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 "Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia"]. ''MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE''. Retrieved 12 April 2023. [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people.]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}MATCHA. [https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 "Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia"]. ''MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE''. Retrieved 12 April 2023. Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}MATCHA. [https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437 "Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia"]. ''MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE''. Retrieved 12 April 2023. Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}MATCHA. {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name=":0"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people.]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name=":0"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called {{ill|Shinko-shiki|simple}}. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name=":0"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name=":0"/>

Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. {{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
== See also ==
* [[Seki-juku (Tōkaidō)]] * [[List of Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties]] * [[Intangible cultural heritage]]
== References == {{Reflist}}
== Sources ==
* "Hikiyama in Shinminato" (Shinminato, Toyama [[Board of education]]) published in October 1981. * McPherson, Sean Harland. "Shifting Traditions: Architecture and Sculpture of Chita Peninsula Dashi." PhD Diss. U.C. Berkeley College of Environmental Design, Department of Architecture, 2001. * "Takaoka Mikurayama" (Takaoka City Board of Education) 2000, published on 31 March 2000.

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>

{{Short description|Float that is pulled or carried during a festival in Japan}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}} {{more citations needed|date=February 2022}}
[[File:Dekayama.JPG|thumb|A Dashi float with people riding it and it being pulled by people]] '''Matsuri float''', also known as a '''dashi''' or '''sansha''', is a type of float that is either pulled or carried during a festival in Japan. It is a general term used to refer to any float that is used for this purpose.
Dashi are one of three large structures at Japanese festivals alongside [[Yatai (food cart)|Yatai]], and [[Mikoshi]].<ref name="matcha-2023a">{{Cite web|last=MATCHA|title=Dashi And Yatai (Festival Floats) - Japanese Encyclopedia|url=https://matcha-jp.com/en/4437|access-date=2023-04-12|website=MATCHA - JAPAN TRAVEL WEB MAGAZINE|language=en}}</ref>
The terminology used for Matsuri floats can be inconsistent and varies by region in Japan. Some of the most common names used for these floats include Kasaboko, Danjiri, Yamahoko, Yamakasa, and Hikimono. Furthermore, Dashi and Yatai floats are sometimes called hikiyama and yama.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/> [[File:ToshoguMikoshi5.jpg|thumb|A mikoshi being carried by people]] Dashi floats (山車) are an important component of Japanese festivals, and were originally designed to look like mountains. This reflects the concept of [[Mountain worship]], where people believed that spirits resided in the mountains. The spears and swords that adorn the tops of the dashi serve as markers for these divine spirits, and people ride on top of the dashi to help welcome the gods. Dashi have wheels and are pulled by people, and can carry passengers as well.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Mikoshi is used to carry kami in a procession called [[Shinko-shiki]]. People carry the Mikoshi on their shoulders, while dashi is pulled by people. People are not allowed to ride on a mikoshi because it is only for gods..<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
Dashi floats can be seen in many festivals in Japan, such as the Takayama Matsuri in Gifu Prefecture and the Kanda Matsuri in Tokyo. During the Takayama Matsuri, ten dashi floats go through the city in the day and at night. The Kanda Matsuri has both dashi floats and mikoshi, with people wearing traditional clothes walking through the streets.<ref name="matcha-2023a"/>
